extracted.intended_audience: higher-education instructors and program designers implementing peer mentoring for undergraduate research proposal writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing, recruiting, training, matching, running, and assessing a peer-mentor program to assist undergraduates with research proposal writing. Emphasis is on practical procedures (screening, matching, in-class logistics) and measures of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer mentor recruitment criteria (examples from literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates who want to apply for the mentor’s position must be third year accounting students who have obtained a credit or above in the second year accounting unit involving the computer laboratory sessions. Mentors are selected according to academic performance, the quality of the written application and availability to participate for four weeks of the semester according to the scheduled class timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection factors used in cited studies: year-of-study (3rd year or beyond), prior completion/grades in relevant units, quality of written application, academic performance (GPA thresholds cited, e.g., GPA >= 5.0 on 7-point scale), and availability. Some programs also require enrollment in a mentor training course (e.g., 'Collaborative Learning and Peer Mentoring'). Use these criteria as options depending on program rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening from student assignments (present researcher's approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present researcher screened peer mentors from the assignments they turned in; there was no application form or personal interview. Students' assignments were sorted into three piles (excellent work, trivia/careless mistakes, on the wrong track) and screening began once assignments were submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical low-resource screening: use students' submitted work to identify potential mentors (consistent high-quality work). The three-pile sorting supports objective matching decisions. Note this is less rigorous than formal application/interview processes but is workable in oversized classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer mentor and mentee matching principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer mentors need to be capable of helping their peers answer the questions they have on the assignment errors or suggestions made by the instructor. Matching is based on assignment performance; mentors change according to students' assignment performance. The researcher prioritizes assigning mentees who were 'on the wrong track' to mentors before those who made careless mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match mentors to mentees so mentors have the relevant strengths to address the mentee's specific errors or misconceptions. Use recent assignment performance to drive matches and be flexible: mentors may change over time as students perform differently across assignments. Prioritize high-need mentees first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentor workload limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, one peer mentor will not assist more than 5 mentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overload mentors; five mentees was reported as overwhelming in cited work because of time and scheduling. Allow variance (not all mentors need equal loads) but set an upper cap (recommended ≤5) and monitor mentor strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer mentor training (instructor-led role switch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer mentor training in this study is not a program or workshop; instead it is more like a mentor and mentee relationship between the instructor (mentor) and the peer mentors (mentee). The instructor helps them clarify the mistakes they made prior assigning them to assist their peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If potential mentors lack sufficient mastery, run targeted in-class or out-of-class training where the instructor reviews common errors and clarifies expectations. Training can be informal (role switch) rather than a semester-long course, but the instructor's guidance 'sets the tone' for subsequent mentor-mentee interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-class mentoring time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the assignment difficulty level, the researcher suggested that the peer mentoring time in class should not exceed 20 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate a bounded period within class (≈20 minutes) for peer mentoring to keep sessions focused and manageable; remaining work can be completed outside class. Timeboxing helps coordinate instructor facilitation and class pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor oversight and facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: As peer mentors and mentees work at their own pace on correcting or revising the assignment, it is anticipated that the instructor would serve as a facilitator to answer any questions peer mentors and mentees might raise. It is also very important for the instructor to observe the interaction between peer mentors and mentees. It provides a great chance for the instructors to learn who works well with whom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should introduce mentor-mentee pairs, review common mistakes (e.g., via PowerPoint), observe pair/group work, step in when inaccurate guidance occurs, and use observations to inform future matches and interventions. Instructor presence legitimizes peer feedback and mitigates risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer mentors' marking and submission protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: The present researcher allows the peer mentors to mark the mentees’ papers and accepts those assignments as students’ final version. Peer mentees’ corrected papers are checked and initialed by the peer mentors prior to turning them in. Students are expected to use a red pen to correct the mistakes they have in their assignments according to the instructor’s comments, and then turn in a corrected version along with the old one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear procedures: mentees submit both original and corrected drafts; mentors initial/check corrected copies; require use of distinct marking (red pen); if many corrections were made, require a clean printed copy. These practices document revisions and mentor involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum / experience match
rubrics_metrics.description: For mentors to provide sound advice, mentors and mentee must share the same experience. McLean (2004) revealed that curriculum did matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mentors who have gone through the same curriculum or encountered the same tasks; this improves the relevance of advice. When possible, match on course background or topic familiarity rather than only on grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection based on academic performance and application quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentors are selected according to academic performance, the quality of the written application and availability to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a combination of objective academic measures (GPA, past grades), evidence of communication/reflective ability (written application), and logistical availability to select mentors. Adjust thresholds to program aims (rigorous vs. peer-led support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / availability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates are required to have accessibility to campus for ease in meeting with mentees; availability is a selection criterion in several cited programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and require realistic availability (on-campus presence, compatible schedules). Recognize that mature students who work may have limited meeting options; set expectations about meeting frequency and modalities (in-class, outside class, asynchronous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential challenges and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Common challenges: finding suitable times to meet (scheduling conflicts), mentors experiencing difficulty getting mentees to listen, mentors burdened by checking papers multiple times, mentors giving incorrect information, and mentees expecting the instructor rather than peers to provide guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation strategies: set clear role expectations, cap mentee loads per mentor, require instructor oversight and spot-checking, train mentors on accurate guidance (and when to escalate to instructor), negotiate meeting times early, and document interactions. Use grouping charts to manage assignments and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes / benefits to evaluate program effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer mentoring benefits college students' research proposal writing. Reported benefits include: mentors feel honored and motivated, development of bonds/friendships, improved grasp of APA format, leadership skill gains, and increased sense of belonging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate programs using surveys and reflective prompts addressing both challenges and rewarding experiences. Outcome measures can include improvements in assignment quality, mentee learning gains (e.g., format mastery), mentor skill development, participant enthusiasm, and retention/connectedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical procedures for program evaluation (informed consent & confidentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present researcher informed participants that they have the right to say no and their class grade will not be in jeopardy if they did not want to participate. In addition, their responses will be confidential and no names will be used to protect their identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the mentoring program (surveys, reflections), obtain voluntary informed consent, protect participant confidentiality, and ensure non-coercion (no grade penalty). Document ethical safeguards in reporting results.
